title: Second derivative — concavity
goal: Use the second derivative $f''(x)$ to see which way a graph bends—concave up like a cup $\cup$ ($f'' > 0$) or concave down like a cap $\cap$ ($f'' < 0$)—and find inflection points where the bend flips.

beforeThis.skill: Watch out: a point with $f''(x) = 0$ is only an inflection point if $f''(x)$ actually switches sign from $+$ to $-$ (or $-$ to $+$) as you cross it!

questions.asking: Spot the intervals along the $x$-axis where the curve bends upward ($f''(x) > 0$) and where it bends downward ($f''(x) < 0$).
questions.statement: On the graph below, mark the intervals where $f''(x) > 0$ (i.e. $f(x)$ is concave up) and where $f''(x) < 0$ (i.e. $f(x)$ is concave down).

figures.alt: Smooth curve above the x-axis that starts nearly flat on the left, bends upward as it rises toward the y-axis, bends downward over a rounded peak at the y-axis, briefly bends upward and levels off at a terrace in the first quadrant, and then bends downward as it descends below the x-axis.

questions.asking: Draw the graph of a single function $y = f(x)$ that satisfies all four increasing/decreasing and concavity conditions simultaneously.
questions.statement:
Sketch a curve that is:

  • concave up when $|x| > 5$,
  • concave down when $|x| < 5$,
  • increasing when $x < 0$, and
  • decreasing when $x > 0$.

questions.asking: Think of $f(x) = x^4$ at $x = 0$: even if $f''(c) = 0$, the graph only has an inflection point if $f''(x)$ actually switches sign ($+$ to $-$ or $-$ to $+$) across $c$!
questions.statement: Suppose $f(x)$ is a function whose second derivative exists and is continuous for all real numbers. True or false: if $f''(3) = 0$, then $x = 3$ is an inflection point of $f(x)$.

questions.asking: Compute $f''(x)$, factor it to find where $f''(x) = 0$, and check where $f''(x)$ actually switches sign to find the inflection point(s).
questions.statement: Find all inflection points for the graph of $f(x) = 3x^5 - 5x^4 + 13x$.
